questions.solution:
For $6^m + 9^n \equiv 0 \pmod{5}$:
$6 \equiv 1 \pmod{5}$ and $9 \equiv -1 \pmod{5}$
So $6^m + 9^n \equiv 1 + (-1)^n \pmod{5}$
This equals 0 only when n is odd.
Number of odd n in {1,...,50} = 25, and m can be any of 50 values.
$p = 50 \times 25 = 1250$
For $m + n$ = square of prime, possible values are 4, 9, 25, 49.
$m + n = 4$: 3 pairs
$m + n = 9$: 8 pairs
$m + n = 25$: 24 pairs
$m + n = 49$: 48 pairs
$q = 3 + 8 + 24 + 48 = 83$
$p + q = 1250 + 83 = 1333$

questions.solution:
The set $S = \{1, 2, 3, ..., 11\}$ has 11 elements.
We need to count subsets $B$ with $n(B) \geq 2$ and even product.
A product is even iff at least one element is even.
Equivalently, count complements: a product is odd iff all elements are odd.
The odd numbers in $S$ are $\{1, 3, 5, 7, 9, 11\}$ (6 elements).
Subsets of odd numbers: $2^6 = 64$.
Among these, those with $n(B) \geq 2$ are all except empty set (1) and singletons (6): $64 - 7 = 57$.
Total subsets with $n(B) \geq 2$: $2^{11} - 1 - 11 = 2036$.
Subsets with even product and $n(B) \geq 2$: $2036 - 57 = 1979$.

questions.question: Two players $A$ and $B$ play a series of games of badminton. The player, who wins $5$ games first, wins the series. Assuming that no game ends in a draw, the number of ways, in which player $A$ wins the series is __________.
questions.solution:
Player $A$ wins the series if $A$ wins $5$ games before $B$ wins $5$ games. The series can last for a minimum of $5$ games and a maximum of $9$ games.

If player $A$ wins the series in exactly $n$ games, then $A$ must win the $n$-th game, and $A$ must win exactly $4$ out of the first $n-1$ games. The number of ways this can happen is given by $^{n-1}C_{4}$.

The possible values for $n$ are $5, 6, 7, 8,$ and $9$.

Total number of ways for $A$ to win the series is the sum of the number of ways $A$ can win in $5, 6, 7, 8,$ or $9$ games:

Total ways $= ^{4}C_{4} + ^{5}C_{4} + ^{6}C_{4} + ^{7}C_{4} + ^{8}C_{4}$

Using the property $^{n}C_{r} + ^{n}C_{r-1} = ^{n+1}C_{r}$, we can simplify the sum:
$^{4}C_{4} = ^{5}C_{5}$
$^{5}C_{5} + ^{5}C_{4} = ^{6}C_{5}$
$^{6}C_{5} + ^{6}C_{4} = ^{7}C_{5}$
$^{7}C_{5} + ^{7}C_{4} = ^{8}C_{5}$
$^{8}C_{5} + ^{8}C_{4} = ^{9}C_{5}$

Therefore, the total number of ways is:
$^{9}C_{5} = \dfrac{9!}{5!4!} = \dfrac{9 \times 8 \times 7 \times 6}{4 \times 3 \times 2 \times 1} = 126$

Answer: $126$

Letters: P(3), Q(2), R(2), S(1), T(1), U(1), V(1) — 7 distinct letters.
All distinct: $\binom{7}{4} \times 4! = 840$.
One pair + 2 distinct: choose repeating letter from $\{P,Q,R\}$ (3 ways), choose 2 from remaining 6 ($\binom{6}{2}=15$), arrange $= 4!/2! = 12$. Total $= 3 \times 15 \times 12 = 540$.

One triple + 1 distinct: only P can repeat 3 times, choose 1 from 6, arrange $= 4!/3! = 4$. Total $= 24$.
Answer $= 840 + 540 + 18 + 24 = 1422$.

questions.q: The number of seven-digit numbers, that can be formed by using the digits $1, 2, 3, 5$ and $7$ such that each digit is used at least once, is :
questions.question: The number of seven-digit numbers, that can be formed by using the digits $1, 2, 3, 5$ and $7$ such that each digit is used at least once, is :
questions.solution:
A seven-digit number is to be formed using the $5$ digits $1, 2, 3, 5,$ and $7$. Since each digit must be used at least once, the remaining $2$ places can be filled by either repeating one digit two more times, or repeating two digits one more time each.

This gives rise to two cases for the frequencies of the digits:

Case 1: One digit appears $3$ times and the other four digits appear $1$ time each.
The number of ways to choose the digit that appears $3$ times is $^{5}C_{1}$.
The number of arrangements of these $7$ digits is $\dfrac{7!}{3!}$.
Number of numbers formed in this case = $^{5}C_{1} \times \dfrac{7!}{3!} = 5 \times \dfrac{5040}{6} = 4200$.

Case 2: Two digits appear $2$ times each and the other three digits appear $1$ time each.
The number of ways to choose the two digits that appear $2$ times is $^{5}C_{2}$.
The number of arrangements of these $7$ digits is $\dfrac{7!}{2!2!}$.
Number of numbers formed in this case = $^{5}C_{2} \times \dfrac{7!}{2!2!} = 10 \times \dfrac{5040}{4} = 12600$.

Total number of seven-digit numbers = $4200 + 12600 = 16800$.

Answer: $16800$

Case 2: $\{1,1,2,2,5\}$: $\frac{5!}{2!\cdot 2!} = 30$ arrangements.
$n(P) = 50$. Hence $n(S) + n(P) = 210 + 50 = 260$.

Total $= 240 + 180 + 240 = 660$.

questions.solution:
The number of triangles formed by joining the vertices of an $n$-sided regular polygon is given by $p_n = ^{n}C_{3}$.

Given that $p_{n+1} - p_n = 66$.

$^{n+1}C_{3} - ^{n}C_{3} = 66$

Using the property $^{n+1}C_{r} - ^{n}C_{r} = ^{n}C_{r-1}$, we get:

$^{n}C_{2} = 66$

$\dfrac{n(n-1)}{2} = 66$

$n(n-1) = 132$

$n^2 - n - 132 = 0$

$(n-12)(n+11) = 0$

Since $n$ must be a positive integer, $n = 12$.

The prime factorization of $12$ is $2^2 \times 3$. The distinct prime divisors of $12$ are $2$ and $3$.

The sum of all distinct prime divisors of $n$ is $2 + 3 = 5$.

Answer: $5$

The lift goes up to the $10^{\text{th}}$ floor but does not stop at the $1^{\text{st}}$ and $2^{\text{nd}}$ floors. Thus, the available floors for the persons to exit are from the $3^{\text{rd}}$ to the $10^{\text{th}}$ floor.

Number of available floors = $8$

The number of ways to select $4$ persons out of $9$ to form the first group is $^{9}C_{4}$. The remaining $5$ persons automatically form the second group.

$^{9}C_{4} = \dfrac{9 \times 8 \times 7 \times 6}{4 \times 3 \times 2 \times 1} = 126$

Now, these two distinct groups must exit at two different floors out of the $8$ available floors. The number of ways to assign $2$ different floors to the $2$ groups is $^{8}P_{2}$.

$^{8}P_{2} = 8 \times 7 = 56$

Total number of ways = $126 \times 56 = 7056$

Answer: $7056$

questions.q: The total number of $3$-digit numbers, whose greatest common divisor with $36$ is $2$, is ______.
questions.question: The total number of $3$-digit numbers, whose greatest common divisor with $36$ is $2$, is ______.
questions.solution:
Prime factorisation of $36 = 2 \times 2 \times 3 \times 3$

So, for number having G.C.D with $36$ to be $2$, the number should be odd multiple of $2$ and does not have factor $3$ and $9$

$⇒$Odd multiple of $2$ are

$\left\{102, 106, 110, 114 \ldots \ldots . 998\right\}\left(225\text{numbers}\right)$

$⇒$No. of multiples of $3$ are

$\left\{102, 114, 126 \ldots \ldots . 990\right\}\left(75\text{numbers}\right)$

Which also include multiple of $9$

Hence, Required $= 225 - 75 = 150$

$5$ boys with allotted roll numbers and seat numbers are seated in such a way that no one sits on the allotted seats. The number of ways of such seating arrangement is equal to the derangement of $5$ boys i.e.,

$= 5 ! \left(1 - \dfrac{1}{1 !} + \dfrac{1}{2 !} - \dfrac{1}{3 !} + \dfrac{1}{4 !} - \dfrac{1}{5 !}\right)$

$= 5 ! - 5 ! + 60 - 20 + 5 - 1$

$= 44$
